case_study_insert.main_stem: Helio Cloud Cooperative (HCC) is a cooperative in the cloud-hosting and data-centre sector, employing a workforce of 90. Founded in 2010 by Sofia Almeida, it provides green web-hosting and cloud storage to business clients across the region and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. Helio plans to invest $1,500,000 in a new energy-efficient data centre, financed by a $900,000 bank loan and $600,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $540,000 a year, a variable cost of $10.00 a unit and a selling price of $19.00, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. The cooperative faces two problems: rising energy waste in its server halls and a shortage of qualified technicians.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Data Centre Operations Log — Q3 2025: The facility delivered 24,000 hosting units last quarter with a hardware fault rate of 3.3%, down from 5.1% a year earlier. Client downtime complaints fell from 48 to 26 a month. Average server uptime reached 99.7%. A survey of 380 business clients found 64% would pay up to $0.45 more for green hosting, and 56% check energy credentials. A skills audit shows 25 of 90 technicians need renewable-energy training; accredited courses cost $1,300 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Helio Cloud Cooperative for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs on the $900,000 loan. (2) The minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.20 to $13.93 an hour from April 2026. (3) Electricity and server hardware input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, while cloud services demand grew 7.5% and inflation is 4.1%.

questions.question_text: HCC plans to fund its $1,500,000 energy-efficient data centre with a $900,000 bank loan and $600,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for HCC of using the $600,000 retained profit rather than borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or repayment, so the cooperative avoids adding to the interest payable of 24 ($'000) and keeps the $900,000 loan manageable. With fixed costs of $540,000 a year and 100,000 units to deliver, preserving cash lets Sofia Almeida absorb the 14.2% rise in electricity and hardware costs without raising the $19.00 price.

Point 2: Using reserves avoids further collateral risk and keeps decision-making with the cooperative's members, since no extra lender can impose conditions on the green data centre. It also leaves borrowing capacity for future renewable-energy investment, though heavy use of reserves reduces the cushion available if energy waste pushes costs above plan. For a 90-person cooperative with democratic leadership, keeping $600,000 of reserves under member control also avoids the covenants a larger lender might impose on the green data centre, and leaves room to fund the $1,300 renewable-energy courses for the 25 technicians who need them.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: HCC is promoting its new energy-efficient data centre. Consider trade-press advertising, conference sponsorship, or targeted email marketing to existing clients. Which should HCC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade-press advertising: Ads in cloud and data-centre journals would build awareness of the green centre among infrastructure buyers and reinforce the cooperative's 64% green-hosting appeal. However, print reach is broad and expensive relative to a 90-person cooperative, results are hard to measure, and much of the readership may not be in the regional client base the 380-person survey represents.

Conference sponsorship: Sponsoring an industry event allows live demonstrations and face-to-face trust-building, which suits a technical green-hosting message. The drawbacks are high one-off fees and a narrow audience limited to delegates, so it may not deliver the steady 24,000-unit quarterly volume needed to justify a $1,500,000 centre, and the long lead time delays returns.

Targeted email marketing to existing clients: Using the finding that 56% of 380 clients check energy credentials, Helio can segment its current customer list, promote the new centre cheaply and measure opens and conversions, cross-selling cloud storage at low cost per contact. Results are limited to the existing base and take care to avoid over-mailing, but the audience is already primed. The 99.7% uptime record is a powerful selling point that email can convey to a known audience at almost no marginal cost, unlike print or events.

Recommendation: HCC should choose targeted email marketing to existing clients. It is the lowest-cost, most measurable option for a cooperative with fixed costs of $540,000, reaches buyers who already value green credentials (64% would pay $0.45 more) and can fill the new centre quickly. Trade-press advertising is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and conference sponsorship is rejected as too narrow and slow to sustain the 100,000-unit plan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to HCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in HCC's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in HCC's context with a justified recommendation explaining why trade-press advertising and conference sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: Helio wants to cut energy waste in its server halls. Explain two benefits for HCC of using democratic leadership to involve its technicians.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites Helio's 90 technicians to suggest ways to reduce energy waste, using the practical knowledge of staff who run the servers and satisfying esteem needs (Maslow). Shared ownership of efficiency targets should lower costs that would otherwise erode the $9.00 contribution per unit and support the $1,500,000 green data centre.

Point 2: Involving technicians in decisions raises commitment in a flat cooperative and helps tackle the shortage of qualified technicians by making Helio a more attractive employer. Their ideas can also reduce the 3.3% hardware fault rate and 48 monthly downtime complaints, protecting uptime of 99.7% and the $1,300-per-employee training investment in renewable-energy skills. Democratic involvement also fits the cooperative's ownership model, where technicians are members with a stake in keeping costs low. Their proposals can be tested against the 24,000-unit quarterly output and 99.7% uptime, giving Sofia Almeida a practical way to cut the energy waste that otherwise erodes the $9.00 contribution per unit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: HCC needs more qualified technicians. Consider recruiting technicians externally or training existing staff with $1,300 accredited courses. Which should HCC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment: Hiring qualified technicians brings immediate skills and fresh ideas, closing the gap shown by the 25 of 90 staff needing renewable-energy training without a long learning curve. This supports the 24,000-unit quarterly output and the 99.7% uptime record. The downsides are higher costs — advertising, interviews and pay — and the time new starters need to learn Helio's systems, all while fixed costs of $540,000 and a $900,000 loan constrain the cooperative.

Training existing staff: Paying $1,300 per employee for accredited courses upgrades the 25 technicians and builds loyalty, which suits a cooperative with democratic leadership and aflat structure. It preserves jobs and tailors skills to green hosting, but it takes staff away from the server halls temporarily, risks delaying the new data centre, and may not fill urgent vacancies quickly enough. Helio must also protect the 99.7% uptime and 24,000-unit quarterly output while the $1,500,000 centre opens; losing 25 of 90 technicians to full-time study would risk both, whereas training in rotation keeps the halls staffed. The cooperative's democratic values also favour developing existing members over bringing in outsiders who may not share its green ethos.

Decision: HCC should choose training existing staff with the $1,300 courses, supported by one or two external hires for specialist roles. Training fits the cooperative's values, costs $32,500 for 25 staff — small beside $1,500,000 — and retains staff amid a technician shortage. Pure external recruitment is rejected because it is costlier, disrupts the flat culture and does not address the 25 staff already needing renewable-energy skills.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to HCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in HCC's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in HCC's context with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture and skills.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HCC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $540,000 ÷ ($19.00 − $10.00) = $540,000 ÷ $9.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Average total cost = Fixed cost per unit + Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $540,000 ÷ 100,000 units + $10.00 = $5.40 + $10.00 = $15.40. Answer: average total cost is $15.40 a unit.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HCC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 60,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units gives a margin of safety of 40,000 units, showing how far demand can fall before losses, which guides use of the $900,000 loan.
2. Average total cost of $15.40 against a $19.00 price shows headroom per unit and helps judge whether the 64% of 380 clients willing to pay $0.45 more for green hosting can be converted.
3. Contribution of $9.00 per unit sets the volume needed to service the $900,000 loan and the $1,500,000 centre, so managers can test the 100,000-unit plan before expanding further.
4. Tracking unit cost against the 3.3% hardware fault rate and 24,000 quarterly units helps target the 25 technicians needing training and decide whether $1,300 courses are worthwhile amid 14.2% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Average total cost = $15.40 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 100,000-unit output; cost headroom vs $19.00 price; loan servicing for the $900,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking against 3.3% fault rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HCC's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed for 2024 and 2025. Which ratio gives the strongest evidence of improvement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings (all figures $'000): 2024 gross margin = 525 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 35.0%; 2025 = 720 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 40.0%. Operating return on sales 2024 = 180 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 12.0%; 2025 = 270 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 15.0%. Return on capital 2024 = 180 ÷ 1,125 × 100 = 16.0%; 2025 = 270 ÷ 1,350 × 100 = 20.0%. Cost of sales rose from 975 to 1,080 while revenue grew from 1,500 to 1,800.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so HCC's financial position has strengthened. The gross margin rising from 35.0% to 40.0% shows better control of direct costs despite 14.2% electricity and hardware inflation, and the operating return on sales climbing from 12.0% to 15.0% indicates the flat 90-person cooperative is absorbing overheads more effectively as revenue grows. Return on capital improved from 16.0% to 20.0%, so the 1,125 to 1,350 of capital employed is being used more productively, supporting the $1,500,000 centre. The strongest evidence is the 20.0% return on capital, because it shows the larger capital base is generating higher returns rather than profit merely tracking sales. A caveat is interest payable rising from 24 to 30 as the $900,000 loan is serviced.

Conclusion: HCC's financial position has improved on every measure, with the rise in return on capital from 16.0% to 20.0% the clearest sign of value creation; the growing interest burden from the $900,000 loan is the main risk to monitor.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the strongest evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HCC of switching its server halls to renewable energy to cut energy waste.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Renewable power would reduce the energy waste that erodes the $9.00 contribution per unit and reinforce the green brand that 64% of 380 clients will pay $0.45 more for, with 56% checking energy credentials. It strengthens the case for the $1,500,000 energy-efficient data centre and may lower exposure to the 14.2% rise in electricity input costs.

Disadvantage: Installing renewable systems adds capital cost and risk on top of the $900,000 loan and fixed costs of $540,000, with no guarantee of immediate savings. With 25 of 90 technicians needing renewable-energy training at $1,300 each and a shortage of qualified staff, the switch could disrupt the 99.7% uptime record and the 24,000-unit quarterly output if reliability falls during transition. HCC should pilot the switch against the 24,000-unit quarterly output and 3.3% fault rate, so that reliability is not sacrificed for brand appeal while the $900,000 loan is being repaid and the 99.7% uptime record is preserved.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in electricity input costs will affect HCC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): The $900,000 loan is explicitly variable-rate, so the extra 0.75% costs 0.75% × $900,000 = $6,750 a year — small against fixed costs of $540,000 and interest payable of 30 ($'000). Higher rates could raise future borrowing costs for the $1,500,000 centre, but Helio can partly hedge by fixing the rate or repaying debt from the $600,000 retained profit.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.93 an hour): The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The sound judgement is qualitative: with a workforce of 90, a compulsory rise lifts costs that cannot be avoided and squeezes the $9.00 contribution per unit unless productivity or the $19.00 price rises. The 64% of 380 clients willing to pay $0.45 more for green hosting offers one route to recovery.

Electricity input costs (14.2%): Helio's $10.00 variable cost is affected by power, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $10.00 rose 14.2%, that is 14.2% × $10.00 = $1.42 per unit, and at 100,000 units about $142,000 a year. Even a $0.45 rise would be $45,000 a year, cutting contribution toward $8.55 and threatening the 99.7% uptime as cost pressure builds.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in electricity input costs will have the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 100,000 units and directly erodes the contribution that funds the $1,500,000 centre. The wage rise matters but cannot be quantified from the insert, and the roughly $6,750 interest effect is small; HCC should invest in efficient cooling and pursue the $0.45 green premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HCC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HCC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in HCC's context with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons why the other two are smaller.
